title: Exact finite-iteration reachability for Bellman operators
formal: Is there an algorithm that, given a finite rational Markov decision process with no end components, its reachability Bellman operator \(\Phi:[0,1]^d\to[0,1]^d\), and rational vectors \(s,t\in[0,1]^d\), decides whether \(\Phi^n(s)=t\) for some integer \(n\geq0\)? The dimension is unbounded and several actions may be available, including several actions tight at the fixed point.
why: Exact attainment is a sharper verification property than convergence of value iteration. Resolving it for Bellman operators would locate how much decidability survives the structured maxima of affine probability updates, beyond the already solved two-dimensional and single-policy cases.
status_note: The 2025 primary paper explicitly leaves arbitrary-dimensional BOR open under its no-end-component promise. A bounded 13 September 2026 later-work check did not locate a resolution. The source’s general-semigroup remark is retained only within its Bellman/product-family setting; general matrix-semigroup undecidability is not treated as a solution.

importance.reason: A precise decidability boundary for structured piecewise-affine dynamics, motivated by finite termination of quantitative value iteration and multiple optimal actions.

sentences: The input describes a finite rational Markov decision process and two rational value vectors.
Its Bellman operator updates each coordinate by the best available affine probability expression.
The question asks whether exact iteration reaches the target vector after finitely many steps.
The source assumes no end components but allows several actions tight at the fixed point.
Convergence and the known two-dimensional decision procedure do not settle the general finite-attainment problem.

definitions: A Markov decision process (MDP) has finitely many states, a designated target sink \(g\), and a finite set of available actions at each other state. Sinks have no actions. Each available action \(a\) at state \(i\) has rational probabilities \(p(i,a,j)\geq0\), summing to one over all states \(j\). An end component consists of a nonempty state subset \(U\) and a nonempty choice of available actions at each state in \(U\), such that all their positive-probability successors stay in \(U\), and the directed graph of these chosen positive-probability transitions is strongly connected. The input promise excludes all such end components. Let \(Q=\{1,\ldots,d\}\) consist of the non-target states from which a path of positive-probability transitions to \(g\) exists. Other non-target states have reachability value zero and are omitted from the vector coordinates. For every \(i\in Q\), define \(L_{i,a}(x)=p(i,a,g)+\sum_{j\in Q}p(i,a,j)x_j\) and \(\Phi(x)_i=\max_{a\in\mathrm{Act}(i)}L_{i,a}(x)\). Each such action set is nonempty. The maximum is coordinatewise: different coordinates may attain it at different actions. All probabilities, the explicit transition tables and the vectors \(s,t\) are inputs with binary rational encodings; \(d\) is the number of retained coordinates. Iteration is \(\Phi^0(s)=s\) and \(\Phi^{n+1}(s)=\Phi(\Phi^n(s))\). Equality means equality of every rational coordinate at one finite iteration, without a numerical tolerance. An action is tight at a fixed point \(u\) when \(L_{i,a}(u)=u_i\). The no-end-component promise gives a unique fixed point and convergence of all iterations to it; no uniqueness of tight actions is assumed. A decision procedure is one deterministic Turing machine halting on every valid input; no time bound or bound on the witnessing \(n\) is imposed.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a terminating exact reachability algorithm on this entire promised class, or prove in Lean that the decision problem on this class is undecidable. Merely computing or approximating the fixed point, deciding whether a limit equals the target, or solving unrestricted matrix-semigroup reachability does not decide finite-iteration reachability of the specified Bellman operator.

context_blocks.text: Convergence does not imply that an iteration ever attains its limit. For \(\Phi(x)=(x+1)/2\), starting at zero produces \(1-2^{-n}\); the fixed point one is approached forever and never reached at a finite step. This scalar map is a valid reachability Bellman operator for a state that either repeats or reaches the target, each with probability one half.

The source proves decidability in arbitrary dimension when the requested vector differs from the unique fixed point. It also handles a fixed-point target when the starting vector is comparable to it coordinatewise, meaning all coordinates lie on the same side of their respective target values.

In dimension two, the paper resolves the remaining incomparable case as well. Thus the outstanding general question permits higher-dimensional starts with some coordinates above and others below their target values, and permits several tight actions.

If every coordinate has a unique tight action, the local fixed-point dynamics reduce to powers of one rational matrix. Proposition 27 gives a finite bound for testing whether these powers send a difference vector to zero. With multiple tight actions, the maximizing matrix can change during the iteration.

The associated matrices have nonnegative entries and row sums at most one. Their available rows can be chosen independently at each coordinate, forming the source’s product family. The resulting map takes coordinatewise maxima; it does not permit an arbitrary favorable sequence of matrices irrespective of those maxima.

The exclusion of end components is part of the target, not an incidental computational convenience. An MDP transformation preserving the least fixed point need not preserve the exact sequence of iterates from a supplied vector. General piecewise-affine undecidability results therefore require an actual reduction into this promised Bellman class before they could answer the question.
